steps.prompt: What is the difference between will and might?
options: Will is quite sure; might is possible but not certain.
Will is used for people; might is used for things.
They mean exactly the same and are interchangeable.
steps.answer: Will is quite sure; might is possible but not certain.
steps.why: Will = I am fairly sure. Might = it is possible, perhaps 50%.

steps.title: will and might
steps.html:
will — quite suremight — possible
+Fares will get cheaper.Fares might get cheaper.
–Cycling won’t replace the car.Cycling might not replace the car.
?Will the trains be faster?— (we do not ask with might)
short answerYes, they will. / No, they won’t.—
with an adverbIt will probably cost more.It could well cost more.

Will and might are followed by the base form, with no to: will get, not will to get.

They are the same for every person: I will, she will, they will — no -s.

The negative of will is won’t; the negative of might is might not.

Make the prediction softer with probably or I think: It will probably cost more. I think buses will get cheaper. Probably goes after will but before won’t: It probably won’t happen.

In Lesson 25 you will put will and might after if: If you don’t hurry, you’ll miss it.

steps.title: The future of getting around
steps.html:
Three things that have already started.

Reading

Nobody knows what our cities will look like in 2045. But three things have already started, and they will probably decide it.

The first is the bus. Buses are greener than they were: they use less fuel, they are quieter, and in most European cities they now create far less pollution than a car with one person in it. City governments have understood this. Bus lanes will get longer and fares might get cheaper, because a full bus takes forty cars off the main road.

The second is the bicycle. Twenty years ago a cycle lane was unusual. Today it is normal in Copenhagen, Bogotá and Almaty. Cycling won’t replace the car for a family of five with luggage, but for one person going four kilometres it is faster than driving and it never sits in a traffic jam.

The third is the train. High-speed lines are expensive, and they take years, but they are reliable and they carry more people per hour than any road. Japan’s Maglev will connect Tokyo and Osaka in 2045, and it might cost 51 billion dollars. Nobody in Japan thinks that is too much.

So what will your journey to work look like in twenty years? Probably not a flying car. More likely: a convenient bus you don’t have to think about, a bike for four kilometres, and a train for four hundred.
